prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, trapping atoms at a magic wavelength to reach fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: B030 is the only candidate that seven of eight members ranked and the only one with two first places and four top-three placements, but I do not rest the case on that count. On the science, it is a measurement achievement of the kind I trust: a clean idea (the magic wavelength that cancels the lattice light shift), a quantitative demonstration, and a thorough control of systematics (blackbody shift, collisions, lattice light shifts) that took the instrument to about 10^-18. It has been reproduced and surpassed in independent laboratories in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Braunschweig and elsewhere, and clock comparisons agree at that level. Its consequences reach beyond metrology: relativistic redshift at millimetre scales, searches for variation of constants and dark matter, and the redefinition of the second now under discussion. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, since Katori proposed and first demonstrated the scheme and Ye drove it to the accuracy and many-body regime, and every colleague who proposed laureates named exactly these two. Having placed IceCube first myself, I accept that a consensus prize is better built on B030, where maturity, attribution and breadth of support all line up.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes: the 2005 frequency-comb prize (Hall, Hansch) and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems (Wineland) sit next to this work, and a prize for a precision instrument may read as an invention rather than a discovery of a new phenomenon. Pierre Lemonde's group and other early lattice-clock groups are outside the credited names, and the pending SI redefinition means the full societal payoff is still prospective. I am an astroparticle experimentalist and cannot settle fine points of priority in atomic physics myself, so I rely on Eva Lindroth and Stefan Kroll and on expert reviewers there. The citation must be worded to make clear that the contribution is the lattice clock and not the comb or ion-clock work.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B030 first as an instrument that changed what can be measured, notes that Ye was not a 2005 laureate so there is no direct conflict, and ranks IceCube last of his eight as probably slightly early because source identification is still thin.
responses.response: I agree on B030 and on the point about 2005: Hall and Hansch were honoured for the comb, which is a tool the clock uses, not for the lattice clock itself. On IceCube I qualify his timing worry. The 2013 diffuse flux has been confirmed in several channels, and that discovery of the neutrinos themselves does not depend on source identification, so I would call it mature, though I concede the source picture is still thin. That makes IceCube a strong second option, not a reason to reorder ahead of B030.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B030 first, noting the physics rests on atomic polarizability and is stable, and recognises that Hall's 2005 prize makes some members feel the area is partly honoured, while the share between Katori's proposal and Boulder's realisation could be argued.
responses.response: Her atomic-structure judgement carries more weight with me than my own on this question, so I take her two-name configuration as settled. I would answer the 2005 overlap by wording the citation around the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 performance, so that it cannot be read as a second comb prize. On the Katori and Ye share, I see an equal two-person split as defensible: one made the concept and first demonstration, the other brought it to record accuracy, and both steps were decisive.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks CMB precision mapping (B055) first as fully mature and overdue, and IceCube second, while acknowledging that the WMAP versus Planck split and the three-person limit are a genuine allocation problem.
responses.response: I agree that the science is mature, and I ranked B055 third myself. My disagreement is about whether a fair trio exists. Page and Bennett built and calibrated WMAP, Spergel carried the parameter analysis, and Puget leads Planck/HFI, so any three exclude either a satellite team or an instrument builder. With COBE (2006) and the 2019 cosmology prize already given, I would not put B055 ahead of a candidate with a clean two-name attribution until the committee agrees how to share credit between WMAP and Planck. I welcome his view of whether his Bennett, Spergel, Puget trio can be defended on the Planck side.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery first as the unrecognised experimental half of a prize whose theory half was given in 2013, but concedes that Evans, Della Negra and others cannot all be accommodated within three names.
responses.response: I share her view that the experimental discovery is of the highest importance and that detector invention is part of it. My difficulty is that, as she says, the credited list has five names and the three-person limit makes any selection contestable between spokespeople, detector designers and the machine builder. Mature recognition of a collaboration result needs a defensible rule for who stands for thousands of members, and I do not yet see one that the committee would accept, so I keep B017 outside my configuration even though I take its merit as high.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a clock, which is an instrument and precision-measurement achievement, as prize-level given the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether expert reviewers see priority issues for lattice-clock proposals or early demonstrations (for example Lemonde's group) that would change the two-name credit.
Whether IceCube credit can be narrowed to three people fairly given the AMANDA and Baikal precursors, which decides how strongly B020 works as an alternative or later candidate.
Whether the prize could instead be split between B030 and a second, distinct achievement without breaking the three-person limit; I have not found a pairing that keeps both parts fairly credited.
statement.conflict_note: No specific recusal issue is apparent from my profile for B030. For B020 I note that I work in astroparticle physics, am a member of the Fermi-LAT collaboration (which contributed follow-up in the 2017 TXS 0506+056 multi-messenger observations) and know the neutrino-astronomy community, so I have field proximity but no known personal or institutional tie to the credited individuals. I have no apparent connection to Katori or Ye.
